name: Nimbus-Axis
description: Nimbus-Axis is a cool blue-violet giant, its cloud decks banded in slate and lavender, wearing a thin ring of dark debris that catches light like an edge of smoked glass. A single storm—the Axis—turns at the north pole in a perfect hexagonal jet stream, so regular that navigation computers use it as a reference point for the entire outer system.

The dense atmosphere is deceptively serene: winds run fast but laminar, and probes descend through color-graded layers—violet to indigo to black—with barely a shudder before their signals flatten into static. There is no violence here, only depth, pressure, and the strange acoustic hum the whole planet makes, resonating through every hull that comes within a million kilometers.

A navigation beacon has orbited above the polar hexagon for as long as ships have charted this system; its maintenance logs credit three successive governments, none of which can produce transfer records older than forty years. Its signal is flawless. Last year it began appending one extra data packet—a timestamp counting down from a figure roughly equal to the hexagon's age.

Helium-3 skimmers work Nimbus's outer bands profitably and without incident, which unsettles veterans more than danger would: nothing here attacks, fails, or changes except the countdown. The consortium's contract renewals are stalled because every crew that rotates home gives the same reason, in the same words, though they have never compared notes: the beacon is not counting down to something happening. It is counting down to something arriving.
